title: Milder with others
hook: look at your own faults and you'll be gentler with others' (On Anger 2.28)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Plato's raised hand, frozen mid-blow. Your line was the raised hand. Did you catch a gesture halfway and hold it? Day five hundred six.

Someone cuts you off in traffic, and you're furious: who drives like that? Ten minutes later you drift into the next lane without signaling, and somehow that was different. You were in a hurry. You had a reason. We are expert lawyers for ourselves and stern judges of everyone else. Seneca saw this clearly, and in the second book of On Anger he offers a cure that has nothing to do with breathing or waiting. It's a kind of honesty. Turn the same light you shine on others, he says, back on yourself. Today: milder with others.
screen: `WHO DRIVES LIKE THAT?` → `TEN MINUTES LATER, YOU DO.` → `LAWYER FOR ME, JUDGE FOR YOU.`

segments.voice: First, nobody is innocent. If we want to judge fairly, Seneca says, let's first agree on this: none of us is without fault. Not one. If you examine yourself honestly, you won't find a person who could be acquitted of everything. Second, eyes in front, faults behind. Seneca's picture: we keep other people's faults before our eyes, and our own behind our back. We see theirs all day. Ours are carried where we can't see them. He lists examples: a tyrant angry at a murderer, a temple robber punishing a theft. Third, the softening. This isn't meant to make you feel worse about yourself. It's meant to make you gentler. When you remember you've done something similar, Seneca says, the anger loses its footing. You'll say: I've done this too. And you'll be milder. Fourth, a neighbor. Some sayings travel. In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus asks in the King James words: why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother's eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye? A speck of sawdust and a plank. Two teachers of the same century, in the same empire, from very different places, reaching for the same kind of picture. Neither borrowed from the other, as far as we know. The insight seems to keep arriving on its own, wherever people are honest about how they judge.
screen: `NONE OF US IS WITHOUT FAULT.` · `THEIRS IN FRONT, OURS BEHIND.` · `I'VE DONE THIS TOO.` · `THE MOTE AND THE BEAM.` · then, large: `MY FAULTS TOO.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who annoyed you recently. Name what they did, plainly. Now gently look behind your own back. When have you done something like it? Maybe not the same, but in the same family: late, careless, short-tempered, unfair. Let one memory come. Don't punish yourself for it. Just hold the two side by side: their fault, your fault. Notice whether the anger toward them softens, even a little. The bell holds the time.
Milder with others. Seneca's cure in On Anger: we see others' faults in front of us and carry our own behind us. Turn around, and you'll judge more gently. Today's word.
Your line: my faults too. Before you judge someone today, out loud or in your head, remember one time you did something like it. Then decide. Day five hundred six.

howItsDone: Some readers of Seneca pause before judging someone to recall a similar fault of their own, as a way to soften anger into fairness.

fork.setup: a coworker misses a deadline and you're about to complain loudly. what does Seneca suggest first?
options: remember a time you missed one too.
fork.reveal: look behind your own back first; remembering your faults makes you milder with others'.

original.note: Latin, 'faults, vices': what Seneca says we keep in front for others and behind for ourselves.

trapdoor: what you thought: be less judgmental because it's polite.
what it means: Seneca says honest self-examination finds no one without fault, and that makes anger lose its footing.
what a scholar hears: Seneca's line puts others' vices 'in oculis' and ours 'a tergo', before the eyes and behind the back; he and the Gospel writers belong to the same first-century Roman world.
